doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Swing rhythm sections in new styles; staff orchestras and live music disappearing
summary: Early bebop and rock still had swing rhythm sections; staff orchestras and live music were everywhere then.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You hear that in early bebop — “Shaw-nuff” you hear Dizzy and Bird playing bebop and the rhythm section is, if I remember right, Cozy Cole and Slam Stewart and Clyde Hart and they’re playing swing, the same thing.

But at that time the music changed, you know. And for a long time older kind of pop music kind of coexisted and then gradually rock ‘n roll won out altogether. Things were very different. It wasn’t just abstract notions of style and aesthetics, it was the fact that

the economics were different, that there were staff orchestras where you could be working for a pretty decent weekly salary as a staff musician. Those don’t exist anymore. There were staff orchestras in California — the film studios had their own orchestras — MGM for example. And live music was everywhere. There were always live bands playing or at least pianists or least organists or at least something playing everywhere you looked. This was very different from now, when most music you hear is synthesized or prerecorded.
